lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Summarising data
lessons.overview: Statistics turns raw data into useful measures and displays so that patterns can be compared.
keyPoints: Mean is total divided by count.
Median is the middle ordered value.
Range is highest minus lowest.

example.question: Find the mean of 4, 6, 6 and 8.
steps: Add the values: 24.
Divide by four values.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Right-triangle ratios
lessons.overview: Sine, cosine and tangent connect an acute angle to the sides of a right-angled triangle.
keyPoints: SOH gives sine = opposite/hypotenuse.
CAH gives cosine = adjacent/hypotenuse.
TOA gives tangent = opposite/adjacent.

example.question: A right triangle has opposite side 6 cm and hypotenuse 10 cm. Find sin θ.
steps: Use sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.
Calculate 6 ÷ 10.

lessons.subject: Mathematics
lessons.title: Angles in polygons
lessons.overview: Angle rules let you find unknown angles from the structure of lines, triangles and polygons.
keyPoints: Angles in a triangle total 180°.
Angles on a straight line total 180°.
Interior angles of an n-sided polygon total (n − 2) × 180°.

example.question: Find the third angle of a triangle with angles 50° and 65°.
steps: Add the known angles: 115°.
Subtract from 180°.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Forces and acceleration
lessons.overview: A resultant force changes an object's motion; Newton's second law connects force, mass and acceleration.
keyPoints: Resultant force is the vector sum of forces.
F = ma.
Balanced forces produce no acceleration.

example.question: Find the acceleration of a 5 kg mass under a 20 N resultant force.
steps: Use a = F ÷ m.
Calculate 20 ÷ 5.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Current, voltage and resistance
lessons.overview: Electric current is charge flow, voltage transfers energy, and resistance opposes the current.
keyPoints: V = IR.
Current is the same through series components.
Voltage is the same across parallel branches.

example.question: A 6 Ω resistor carries 2 A. Find the voltage.
steps: Use V = IR.
Multiply 2 by 6.

lessons.subject: Physics
lessons.title: Wave speed and behaviour
lessons.overview: Waves transfer energy through oscillations and are described by frequency, wavelength and speed.
keyPoints: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.
Frequency is measured in hertz.
Reflection changes direction but not frequency.

example.question: A 5 Hz wave has wavelength 3 m. Find its speed.
steps: Use v = fλ.
Multiply 5 by 3.

lessons.subject: Biology
lessons.title: Genes and inheritance
lessons.overview: Genes are DNA sections whose alleles help determine inherited characteristics.
keyPoints: Genotype is the allele combination.
Phenotype is the observed characteristic.
A dominant allele is expressed in a heterozygote.

example.question: Cross two heterozygous Tt parents. What fraction is tt?
steps: List each parent's gametes: T and t.
A Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt.

lessons.subject: Biology
lessons.title: Energy in ecosystems
lessons.overview: Food chains and webs show feeding relationships and the direction of energy transfer.
keyPoints: Producers capture energy to make food.
Arrows point from food to consumer.
Energy is lost between trophic levels.

example.question: In grass → grasshopper → frog, identify the primary consumer.
steps: The producer is grass.
The organism that eats the producer is the primary consumer.

lessons.subject: Biology
lessons.title: The circulatory system
lessons.overview: The heart and blood vessels form a double circulation that supplies cells and removes wastes.
keyPoints: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
Veins carry blood toward the heart.
Capillaries have thin walls for exchange.

example.question: Why are capillary walls one cell thick?
steps: Materials must diffuse between blood and tissues.
A thin wall shortens the diffusion distance.
example.answer: It allows rapid exchange of substances.

lessons.subject: Chemistry
lessons.title: Acids, bases and neutralisation
lessons.overview: Acids donate hydrogen ions in water, while bases accept them or supply hydroxide ions.
keyPoints: pH below 7 is acidic.
Acid + base forms salt + water.
Indicators change colour across pH ranges.

example.question: Name the salt from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.
steps: Hydrochloric acid forms chloride salts.
The base supplies sodium ions.

lessons.subject: Chemistry
lessons.title: How atoms bond
lessons.overview: Atoms form ionic, covalent or metallic bonds, and the bonding explains material properties.
keyPoints: Ionic bonding transfers electrons.
Covalent bonding shares electron pairs.
Metallic bonding has positive ions in delocalised electrons.

example.question: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity?
steps: Conduction needs mobile charged particles.
Its ions are fixed in a crystal lattice when solid.

lessons.subject: Chemistry
lessons.title: Hydrocarbons and homologous series
lessons.overview: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds; homologous series share a functional group and general formula.
keyPoints: Alkanes have only single carbon bonds.
Alkenes contain a C=C bond.
Members of a series have similar chemical properties.

example.question: Is C₂H₄ an alkane or alkene?
steps: Alkanes follow CnH2n+2; for n=2 that is C₂H₆.
C₂H₄ follows the alkene formula CnH2n.

lessons.subject: English
lessons.title: Reading for evidence
lessons.overview: Strong comprehension answers combine the passage's explicit facts with careful inference.
keyPoints: Read the question before locating evidence.
Use context to infer unfamiliar words.
Support an inference with details from the passage.

example.question: A character shuts every window as clouds gather. What can you infer?
steps: Connect the clouds with likely rain.
Closing windows prevents rain entering.

lessons.subject: English
lessons.title: Building a clear essay
lessons.overview: A clear essay develops one central response through organised paragraphs and relevant evidence.
keyPoints: Plan a precise thesis before writing.
Give each paragraph one controlling idea.
Link evidence back to the question.

example.question: What should follow a paragraph's topic sentence?
steps: The topic sentence states the claim.
The claim needs support and explanation.

lessons.subject: English
lessons.title: Speech sounds and stress
lessons.overview: Oral English depends on accurate sound contrasts, syllable stress and intonation.
keyPoints: A syllable contains one vowel sound.
Stress makes one syllable more prominent.
Intonation is the rise and fall of pitch.

example.question: Which syllable is stressed in REcord when it is a noun?
steps: Say the noun naturally.
The first syllable is stronger.

lessons.subject: Economics
lessons.title: Competition and market power
lessons.overview: Market structure depends on the number of firms, entry barriers, product differences and control over price.
keyPoints: Perfect competition has many price-taking firms.
A monopoly has one dominant supplier.
Oligopoly has a few interdependent firms.

example.question: Why can a monopolist influence price?
steps: It is the sole or dominant supplier.
Consumers have few close substitutes.

lessons.subject: Economics
lessons.title: Functions of money and banks
lessons.overview: Money enables exchange and valuation, while financial institutions move savings toward borrowing and investment.
keyPoints: Money is a medium of exchange.
Commercial banks accept deposits and make loans.
Central banks manage currency and monetary policy.

example.question: Which function lets prices be compared?
steps: Prices express each product's value in the same measure.
That function is called a unit of account.

lessons.subject: Economics
lessons.title: Measuring development
lessons.overview: Development combines rising material living standards with wider improvements in health, education and opportunity.
keyPoints: Real GDP per person measures average output.
HDI combines income, health and education.
Growth can occur without equal development.

example.question: Why is GDP per person alone incomplete?
steps: It is an average and may hide inequality.
It omits health, education and environmental quality.
example.answer: It misses distribution and non-income wellbeing.

lessons.subject: Computer Science
lessons.title: How networks communicate
lessons.overview: Networks connect devices so they can exchange data and share resources through agreed protocols.
keyPoints: A LAN covers a limited area.
Routers forward packets between networks.
Protocols define communication rules.

example.question: What device forwards data between a home LAN and the internet?
steps: The data must cross between different networks.
A router selects the route for packets.

lessons.subject: Computer Science
lessons.title: Processor, memory and storage
lessons.overview: A computer combines processing, temporary working memory and persistent storage.
keyPoints: The CPU executes instructions.
RAM holds active programs and data.
Storage retains data without power.

example.question: Why does adding RAM often improve multitasking?
steps: Running programs need working memory.
More RAM reduces slow transfers to storage.
example.answer: More active data can remain in fast memory.

lessons.subject: Computer Science
lessons.title: Variables and control flow
lessons.overview: Programs store values and use sequence, selection and iteration to transform input into output.
keyPoints: Variables name stored values.
Selection branches on a condition.
Loops repeat a block of instructions.

example.question: Which structure repeats an instruction ten times?
steps: The same step must run a known number of times.
Use a count-controlled loop.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Controls of climate
lessons.overview: Latitude, altitude, winds, ocean currents and distance from the sea shape long-term weather patterns.
keyPoints: Higher latitudes receive less direct sunlight.
Temperature usually falls with altitude.
The sea moderates coastal temperatures.

example.question: Why do coastal places often have a smaller temperature range?
steps: Water heats and cools more slowly than land.
Sea air moderates nearby land temperatures.
example.answer: The ocean reduces seasonal temperature extremes.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Population change and structure
lessons.overview: Births, deaths and migration change population size and age structure.
keyPoints: Natural increase is births minus deaths.
Net migration is immigration minus emigration.
A population pyramid shows age and sex structure.

example.question: A country has 20 births and 8 deaths per thousand. Find natural increase.
steps: Subtract the death rate from the birth rate.
Calculate 20 − 8.

lessons.subject: Geography
lessons.title: Using resources sustainably
lessons.overview: Sustainable resource use meets present needs while protecting future supply and environmental systems.
keyPoints: Renewable resources can replenish naturally.
Conservation reduces waste and damage.
Management balances social, economic and environmental needs.

example.question: Why is solar energy renewable?
steps: Its source is sunlight.
Sunlight is continually replenished on human timescales.
example.answer: Its energy source is naturally renewed.

lessons.subject: Government
lessons.title: Legislature, executive and judiciary
lessons.overview: Government functions are divided among institutions that make, carry out and interpret laws.
keyPoints: The legislature makes laws.
The executive implements policy.
The judiciary interprets law and resolves disputes.

example.question: Which arm reviews whether an action follows the constitution?
steps: The issue requires legal interpretation.
Courts form the judiciary.

lessons.subject: Government
lessons.title: Political parties and representation
lessons.overview: Political parties organise citizens around policies, contest elections and help form governments.
keyPoints: Parties aggregate public interests.
A manifesto presents proposed policies.
Opposition parties scrutinise government.

example.question: What is the purpose of a party manifesto?
steps: Voters need to know what a party proposes.
It states policies and election commitments.
example.answer: To present the party's programme to voters.

lessons.subject: Government
lessons.title: National interests abroad
lessons.overview: Foreign policy guides how a state relates to other states and international organisations.
keyPoints: Security and prosperity are common interests.
Diplomacy manages relations peacefully.
Treaties create agreed international obligations.

example.question: Why do states maintain embassies?
steps: States need continuous official communication abroad.
Embassies support diplomacy and citizens.
example.answer: To conduct diplomatic relations and represent national interests.

lessons.subject: Literature
lessons.title: How drama creates meaning
lessons.overview: Drama develops conflict through dialogue, action, stage directions and performance before an audience.
keyPoints: Dialogue reveals character and advances action.
Stage directions guide performance.
Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows more than a character.

example.question: Why can dramatic irony create tension?
steps: The audience anticipates a danger or consequence.
The character acts without that knowledge.
example.answer: The audience foresees what the character cannot.

lessons.subject: Literature
lessons.title: Voice, imagery and rhythm
lessons.overview: Poetry compresses meaning through deliberate sound, image, line and speaker choices.
keyPoints: The speaker is the voice within the poem.
Imagery appeals to the senses.
Rhythm and line breaks shape pace and emphasis.

example.question: What does repeated harsh consonant sound often affect?
steps: Notice how the sound feels when spoken.
Connect that sound to mood or emphasis.
example.answer: It can create a forceful or tense effect.

lessons.subject: Literature
lessons.title: Narrator and point of view
lessons.overview: A prose narrator controls what readers know and influences how events and characters are interpreted.
keyPoints: First-person narration uses I or we.
Third-person limited follows one character's perspective.
An unreliable narrator may distort events.

example.question: What is one effect of first-person narration?
steps: Events are filtered through one participant.
Readers gain close access to that person's thoughts.
example.answer: It creates intimacy but limits knowledge to the narrator.
